Sinotrans Shanghai Company v. Shenzhen Jiangnan Economic Development Corporation — dispute over freight forwarding contract

Plaintiff: Sinotrans Shanghai Company (hereinafter referred to as Sinotrans Shanghai).

Legal Representative: Yang Dazu, General Manager.

Agent ad litem: Wang Juncui, Cadre of Sinotrans Shanghai Company.

Agent ad litem: Chen Xinggen, Lawyer of Shanghai Huizhong Law Firm.

Defendant: Shenzhen Jiangnan Economic Development Corporation (hereinafter referred to as Jiangnan Corporation).

Legal Representative: Yang Lian, General Manager.

Agent ad litem: Deng Yuanhui and Liang Xiaochuan, Lawyers of Shenzhen Special Zone Economic and Trade Law Firm.

The plaintiff, Sinotrans Shanghai Company (hereinafter referred to as Sinotrans Shanghai), filed a lawsuit with the Shanghai Maritime Court against the defendant, Shenzhen Jiangnan Economic Development Corporation (hereinafter referred to as Jiangnan Corporation), concerning a dispute over a freight forwarding contract.

Plaintiff's Allegations: In March 1990, the defendant Jiangnan Corporation entrusted the plaintiff with the customs declaration, cargo booking, and shipment of acetonitrile to Baltimore, USA. After completing the customs formalities, the plaintiff loaded the goods onto the vessel and shipped them on time. Because the defendant did not indicate on the power of attorney whether freight was prepaid or collect, the plaintiff was unable to specify the freight payment method on the bill of lading. In accordance with shipping practice, the carrier vessel company treated all bills of lading that did not specify the freight payment method as freight prepaid and collected USD 25,568 from the plaintiff. Subsequently, the plaintiff repeatedly requested the defendant to pay this freight, but payment was refused. In December 1992, the plaintiff and the defendant reached an agreement, whereby the defendant agreed to settle the freight by the end of May 1993. Despite this, the defendant still failed to pay. The plaintiff requested that the defendant reimburse the freight advanced by the plaintiff in the amount of USD 25,568, together with interest for two and a half years from August 4, 1990, amounting to USD 3,315.58 (calculated at an annual interest rate of 5.1875%).

Defendant's Defense: In March 1990, the defendant acted as an agent for Shenzhen Haiwan Petrochemical Industry Corporation (hereinafter referred to as Haiwan Corporation) in exporting acetonitrile. The defendant was responsible for customs declaration, while Haiwan Corporation assisted with out-of-region customs declaration and other related matters. The domestic and foreign trade contracts and relevant documents indicated the price term as FOB. The defendant affixed its official seal to blank freight forwarding powers of attorney and handed them to Haiwan Corporation, which then delivered them to the plaintiff. However, the plaintiff's handling officer omitted to fill in the price term FOB on the power of attorney; the fault lies with the plaintiff. Although the parties subsequently signed an agreement to settle the freight, this constituted a material misunderstanding on the part of the defendant regarding the content of the act and should be invalidated. The plaintiff's claim has exceeded the statute of limitations and should be dismissed. Haiwan Corporation has an interest in this case, and the court should notify it to participate in the proceedings as a third party without independent claims.

After trial, the Shanghai Maritime Court found the following facts: In February 1990, Haiwan Corporation entered into an acetonitrile purchase and sale contract with Hong Kong Dongruhang Company Limited, with Haiwan Corporation as the seller. To perform the purchase and sale contract, Haiwan Corporation entrusted the defendant Jiangnan Corporation to act as its export agent. Jiangnan Corporation and Haiwan Corporation agreed that Jiangnan Corporation would be responsible for export customs declaration, and Haiwan Corporation would assist with out-of-region customs declaration; Haiwan Corporation would be responsible for matters concerning goods quality, transportation, and urging the opening of letters of credit. In March of the same year, Jiangnan Corporation entered into a sales contract with Hong Kong Dongruhang Company Limited, with Jiangnan Corporation as the seller, and the goods were to be shipped from Shanghai via Hong Kong to US ports. The above foreign trade contract, customs declaration, letter of credit, and invoice all indicated the price term as FOB Shanghai. Thereafter, Jiangnan Corporation affixed its company seal on the "Principal" section of a blank freight forwarding power of attorney and handed it to Haiwan Corporation to be forwarded to the plaintiff, Sinotrans Shanghai, entrusting it with customs declaration, cargo booking, and shipment tasks. After accepting the freight forwarding entrustment, Sinotrans Shanghai handled customs declaration and cargo booking, and in May of the same year arranged for the goods to be shipped to Baltimore, USA, on voyage 9020 of the vessel "NEWHAITENG". Because Jiangnan Corporation did not indicate the freight payment method on the freight forwarding power of attorney, Sinotrans Shanghai also did not indicate it on the bill of lading. In accordance with shipping practice, the carrier treated all bills of lading that did not indicate the freight payment method as freight prepaid and collected USD 25,568 from Sinotrans Shanghai. Subsequently, on August 4 of the same year, Sinotrans Shanghai issued a charge account and requested payment from Haiwan Corporation, which was refused. Then in June and July 1992, Sinotrans Shanghai requested payment from Jiangnan Corporation, which was also refused. In December of the same year, Sinotrans Shanghai and Jiangnan Corporation reached a repayment agreement: Jiangnan Corporation confirmed entrusting Sinotrans Shanghai with the agency for export space allocation and transportation business and agreed to pay the freight to Sinotrans Shanghai by May 31, 1993. When the time came, Jiangnan Corporation still did not pay.

The Shanghai Maritime Court held that the sales contract and the freight forwarding contract are two separate legal relationships. The FOB price term in the sales contract only binds the buyer and seller and does not affect the freight forwarding agent's right to collect from the principal the expenses actually incurred in the agency, including expenses advanced for the principal's benefit. Jiangnan Corporation served as the export agent of Haiwan Corporation and should have performed civil acts in the name of Haiwan Corporation. However, Jiangnan Corporation entrusted Sinotrans Shanghai with freight forwarding in its own name. Sinotrans Shanghai handled the cargo transportation matters on behalf of Jiangnan Corporation, thereby establishing a freight forwarding contractual relationship with Jiangnan Corporation as the principal and Sinotrans Shanghai as the freight forwarding agent. Article 63, paragraph 2 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC provides: "An agent shall perform civil juristic acts in the name of the principal within the scope of the power of agency. The principal shall bear civil liability for the agent's acts within the scope of the power of agency." As a party to the contract, Jiangnan Corporation shall bear the legal consequences arising therefrom, and Sinotrans Shanghai has the right to collect from Jiangnan Corporation the freight it advanced. In accordance with Article 56, paragraph 2 of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, the outcome of this case has no legal interest in relation to Haiwan Corporation, and the opinion of Jiangnan Corporation to add Haiwan Corporation as a third party without independent claims in the proceedings was not adopted. Jiangnan Corporation also argued that the General Principles of the Civil Law provides that "the limitation of action for requesting protection of civil rights from a people's court is two years." Sinotrans Shanghai issued the freight collection note on August 4, 1990, and filed the lawsuit on August 3, 1993, which has exceeded the statute of limitations. Upon examination, the court found: Although Article 135 of the General Principles of the Civil Law provides that "the limitation of action for requesting protection of civil rights from a people's court is two years," Sinotrans Shanghai first requested payment of freight from Jiangnan Corporation on June 24, 1992. In December 1992, Sinotrans Shanghai and Jiangnan Corporation reached a repayment agreement, with Jiangnan Corporation agreeing to pay the overdue freight to Sinotrans Shanghai. Pursuant to Article 140 of the General Principles of the Civil Law: "The limitation of action shall be interrupted by the filing of an action, the assertion of a claim by one party, or the agreement by one party to perform an obligation. The limitation period shall recommence from the time of the interruption." Accordingly, Sinotrans Shanghai's lawsuit did not exceed the two-year effective period. The defense reason of Jiangnan Corporation regarding a material misunderstanding of the content of the repayment agreement signed by both parties could not be established. The Supreme People's Court's Opinions on Several Issues concerning the Implementation of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the PRC (for Trial Implementation) provides: "A material misunderstanding may be found where an actor, due to a mistaken understanding of the nature of the act, the other party, or the variety, quality, specification, or quantity of the subject matter, causes the consequences of the act to be contrary to his will and results in relatively significant losses." The freight forwarding contractual relationship between Jiangnan Corporation and Sinotrans Shanghai was clear, the agency act had already occurred, and the fact that Sinotrans Shanghai advanced the freight existed. There was no mistaken understanding on the part of the actor (Jiangnan Corporation) regarding the nature of the content of the act (repaying the overdue freight). Accordingly, on March 21, 1994, the Shanghai Maritime Court rendered the following judgment:

The defendant, Shenzhen Jiangnan Economic Development Corporation, shall pay the plaintiff, Sinotrans Shanghai Company, the freight of USD 25,568 and interest of USD 3,315.85.

Court acceptance fee of USD 839.12 shall be borne by Jiangnan Corporation.

The defendant Jiangnan Corporation, dissatisfied with the judgment of first instance, appealed to the Shanghai High People's Court. Jiangnan Corporation's grounds for appeal were: Sinotrans Shanghai failed to fill in the blank freight forwarding power of attorney based on the documents, materials, and price term FOB Shanghai forwarded by Haiwan Corporation, which resulted in the freight being uncollectible, and therefore Sinotrans Shanghai should bear liability; requested that Hong Kong Dongruhang Company Limited be added as a defendant or third party in the proceedings to pursue recovery of the freight; requested that the original judgment be set aside and the case be retried.

Upon trial, the Shanghai High People's Court held: The appellee, Sinotrans Shanghai, implemented specific freight forwarding acts based on the appellant Jiangnan Corporation's freight forwarding power of attorney, which was consistent with the agreement of both parties. Sinotrans Shanghai was not an agent for the foreign trade activities between the appellant and Hong Kong Dongruhang Company Limited. According to the sales contract signed with the buyer, Hong Kong Dongruhang Company Limited, the FOB price term should have required the buyer to arrange cargo booking and shipping and pay the freight. However, Jiangnan Corporation performed the buyer's obligations on its behalf by arranging cargo booking and shipping procedures on its own and failed to indicate the freight payment method on the freight forwarding power of attorney. Therefore, it should pay the freight to the agent. When Jiangnan Corporation submitted a blank power of attorney to Sinotrans Shanghai for handling freight forwarding procedures, it could be deemed that it agreed to bear full responsibility for the actual entrusted matters. Jiangnan Corporation's argument that Sinotrans Shanghai should have filled in the blank freight forwarding power of attorney based on the documents, materials, and price term FOB Shanghai forwarded by Haiwan Corporation, and that the primary fault for this act lay with Sinotrans Shanghai, could not be established. The legal consequences arising therefrom should be borne by Jiangnan Corporation. The judgment of the first instance court was not improper. As for Jiangnan Corporation's request to add Hong Kong Dongruhang Company Limited as a defendant or third party in these proceedings to pursue recovery of the freight, because the relationship between Hong Kong Dongruhang Company Limited and Jiangnan Corporation was a sales contract relationship, which was a different legal relationship from the freight forwarding contract dispute under consideration in this case, it should not be added to participate in these proceedings. The facts found by the first instance judgment were clear, and the application of law was correct. Jiangnan Corporation's grounds for appeal could not be established. Accordingly, on October 31, 1994, the Shanghai High People's Court, pursuant to Article 153, paragraph 1, item (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the PRC, rendered the following judgment:

The appeal of Jiangnan Corporation is dismissed, and the original judgment is affirmed.

Court acceptance fee for the appeal of USD 839.12 shall be borne by Jiangnan Corporation.

Jiangnan Corporation, dissatisfied with the final judgment of the Shanghai High People's Court, filed a petition for retrial with the Shanghai High People's Court on the grounds that Sinotrans Shanghai bore liability for the fault of unclear entrustment and violation of the document delivery procedure, and that the FOB Shanghai price term and the freight forwarding dispute in this case should be considered as a whole.

After reviewing the case, the Shanghai High People's Court held that filling in the freight forwarding power of attorney was the responsibility of the principal, not an obligation of the agent. Jiangnan Corporation submitted a blank freight forwarding power of attorney bearing its company seal to Sinotrans Shanghai, and therefore should bear liability for the fault of unclear entrustment in this case. Sinotrans Shanghai handed over the bill of lading to Tan Qilun, the consignee of the buyer Hong Kong Dongruhang Company Limited, in the presence of Zhou Shiqu, the manager of Haiwan Corporation. Neither the buyer nor the seller raised any objection to this act. Therefore, the document delivery act of Sinotrans Shanghai was not improper. The sales contract and the freight forwarding agency are two separate legal relationships; the former does not affect the payment obligation arising from certain legal facts for the parties to the latter legal relationship. The original judgment was correct in both fact-finding and application of law. Accordingly, on March 22, 1995, the court notified Jiangnan Corporation that its grounds for retrial could not be established and affirmed the original judgment.
